questions.title: Terminal branch of the external carotid artery (superficial temporal)
questions.question: Which one of the following is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lingual artery is one of the external carotid's earlier branches, supplying the tongue, not one of its two terminal branches.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid supplying the face, not one of its two terminal branches.
explanations.C: Correct. The external carotid artery ends, behind the neck of the mandible within the parotid gland, by dividing into its two terminal branches: the superficial temporal artery and the maxillary artery. All of its other named branches (superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular) arise along its course before this terminal division. The superficial temporal artery then continues upward over the zygomatic arch to supply the scalp.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The occipital artery is a branch of the external carotid supplying the back of the scalp, not one of its two terminal branches.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid, arising near its origin, not one of its two terminal branches.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the superficial temporal artery as one of the external carotid artery's two terminal branches.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.62

questions.title: Terminal branch of the external carotid artery (maxillary)
questions.question: One of the following is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The facial artery arises from the external carotid before its terminal division, not as one of the two terminal branches.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lingual artery likewise arises before the terminal division.
explanations.C: Correct. The external carotid artery's two terminal branches are the maxillary artery and the superficial temporal artery, both arising from its division behind the neck of the mandible within the parotid gland. The maxillary artery is the larger of the two and supplies the deep structures of the face, the nasal cavity, the palate and the meninges via the middle meningeal artery. Every other named branch of the external carotid, including superior thyroid, lingual, facial and occipital, arises earlier along its course.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The occipital artery arises from the external carotid's posterior aspect well before the terminal division.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid, arising near its origin.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the maxillary artery as one of the external carotid artery's two terminal branches.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.62

questions.title: First branch of the external carotid artery
questions.question: What is the first branch of the external carotid artery?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lingual artery is the external carotid's second branch, arising above the superior thyroid artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The maxillary artery is one of the external carotid's two terminal branches, arising last, not first.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The facial artery arises after the lingual artery, not first.
explanations.D: Correct. The superior thyroid artery is the first (most inferior) branch of the external carotid artery, arising just above the origin of the external carotid from the common carotid, close to the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. It curves downward to supply the thyroid gland and larynx before the external carotid gives off its remaining branches further up the neck. This first-branch position is a standard landmark used to identify the external carotid at surgery.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superficial temporal artery is one of the external carotid's two terminal branches, arising last, not first.

questions.learning_objective: State that the superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.62

questions.title: Aortic arch branch: brachiocephalic artery
questions.question: Which one of the following arteries arises directly from aortic arch?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right common carotid artery arises from the brachiocephalic artery, not directly from the aortic arch.
explanations.B: Correct. The arch of the aorta gives off three large branches from its upper convex aspect: the brachiocephalic (innominate) artery, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery, in that order from right to left. The brachiocephalic artery is the first and largest of the three, ascending briefly before dividing behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. It is therefore the artery on the right side of the body that arises directly from the arch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The right subclavian artery is a branch of the brachiocephalic artery, not a direct branch of the aortic arch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The external carotid artery is a terminal branch of the common carotid artery, two vessel generations removed from the aortic arch.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The posterior auricular artery is a small branch of the external carotid artery, far downstream of the aortic arch.

questions.learning_objective: State that the brachiocephalic artery arises directly from the aortic arch.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.62

questions.author_notes: Main concept reused from the Kasr 104-CPS lane's own aortic-arch concept (CON-CVS-9C60987F3CB5A1), which already states all three arch branches; see this lane's pending-live overlay.

questions.title: Aortic arch branch: left common carotid artery
questions.question: Which one of the following arteries arises directly from aortic arch?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ascending pharyngeal artery is a small branch of the external carotid artery, far downstream of the aortic arch.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, itself a branch of the subclavian artery, not a direct branch of the aortic arch.
explanations.C: Correct. The aortic arch gives off three branches from its convex upper aspect, in order from right to left: the brachiocephalic artery, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery. Unlike the right common carotid artery, which arises indirectly as a division of the brachiocephalic artery, the left common carotid arises as its own separate, direct branch of the arch. This right/left asymmetry, one side direct and one side via the brachiocephalic trunk, is a key point distinguishing the two common carotid arteries' origins.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The right common carotid artery arises from the brachiocephalic artery, a division of it, not directly from the aortic arch itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The right subclavian artery likewise arises from the brachiocephalic artery, not directly from the aortic arch.

questions.learning_objective: State that the left common carotid artery, unlike the right, arises directly from the aortic arch rather than via the brachiocephalic artery.

questions.title: Internal jugular vein termination
questions.question: Where does the internal jugular vein terminate?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The external jugular vein is a separate, more superficial vein that empties into the subclavian vein, not into the internal jugular vein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Subclavian jugular vein" is not a real named vessel; the internal jugular joins the subclavian vein itself, not a vein of this name.
explanations.C: Correct. The internal jugular vein descends through the neck within the carotid sheath and terminates behind the sternal end of the clavicle by uniting with the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. This union point, the venous angle, is a key surgical and clinical landmark (used for central line placement and as the site the thoracic duct empties into on the left). The internal jugular vein itself does not continue beyond this point.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Common lingual vein" is not the internal jugular vein's termination; the lingual vein is a tributary that joins the internal jugular (often via the common facial vein) higher up in the neck, not its termination point.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The sigmoid sinus is the intracranial structure the internal jugular vein begins as a continuation of, at its upper end, not where it terminates at its lower end.

questions.learning_objective: State that the internal jugular vein terminates by uniting with the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.62

questions.title: External jugular vein termination
questions.question: Where does the external jugular vein terminate?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superior vena cava receives the two brachiocephalic veins, well downstream of where the external jugular vein itself ends.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava drains the lower body and has no connection to the external jugular vein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The brachiocephalic vein is where the internal jugular vein terminates (by uniting with the subclavian vein), not where the external jugular vein itself ends.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This option restates the vessel's own name and is not a termination point.
explanations.E: Correct. The external jugular vein runs superficially down the side of the neck, crossing sternocleidomastoid, and pierces the deep fascia just above the clavicle to empty into the subclavian vein. This is a separate, more superficial drainage route from the internal jugular vein, which instead joins the subclavian vein deep within the carotid sheath to form the brachiocephalic vein. The external jugular's termination point, about one and a half inches above the clavicle, is also a recognised clinically "dangerous" point because the vein is tethered open there and can entrain air if injured.

questions.learning_objective: State that the external jugular vein terminates by draining into the subclavian vein.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.63

questions.title: Facial artery origin
questions.question: The facial artery is a branch of which of these arteries?

explanations.A: Correct. The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery, arising just above the lingual artery, looping over the submandibular gland and the lower border of the mandible, and crossing onto the face at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle. It then runs a tortuous course toward the medial angle of the eye, supplying the lower and upper lips, the nose, and much of the superficial face along the way. Its origin from the external, not internal, carotid is consistent with the general rule that the external carotid supplies the face and superficial neck while the internal carotid supplies the brain and orbit.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck and supplies the brain and orbit, not the face.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The common carotid artery divides into the internal and external carotid arteries and gives off no branches of its own in the neck; the facial artery arises from the external carotid, one division beyond the common carotid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The maxillary artery is itself a terminal branch of the external carotid, a separate vessel from the facial artery, not the facial artery's parent vessel.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superficial temporal artery is the other terminal branch of the external carotid, a separate vessel from the facial artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.63

questions.title: Pulse in front of the ear
questions.question: The pulse felt in front of the ear is for which of these arteries?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The external carotid artery lies deeper in the neck and is not the vessel palpated directly in front of the ear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The internal carotid artery has no branches or accessible surface pulse in the neck above the carotid bifurcation and is not palpable in front of the ear.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The common carotid artery's pulse is felt in the neck alongside the larynx, not in front of the ear.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The maxillary artery runs deep to the neck of the mandible and is not palpable at the skin surface in front of the ear.
explanations.E: Correct. The superficial temporal artery, one of the external carotid's two terminal branches, crosses the root of the zygomatic arch just in front of the tragus of the ear before ascending into the scalp. Because it is superficial at this point, its pulse can be readily felt (and used as a landmark, for example to identify the auriculotemporal nerve running alongside it) immediately in front of the ear. This is one of several standard surface-anatomy pulse points tested for the head and neck arteries.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pulse felt in front of the ear is the superficial temporal artery.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.63

questions.title: Pulse in front of sternomastoid
questions.question: The pulse felt in front of sternomastoid ms is for which of these arteries?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The external carotid artery lies more superficially and anteriorly higher in the neck, and is not the vessel classically palpated along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid lower in the neck.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The internal carotid artery lies posterolateral to the external carotid above the bifurcation and is not the vessel this pulse point refers to.
explanations.C: Correct. The common carotid artery's pulse (the carotid pulse) is classically palpated along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, at roughly the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, where the vessel lies relatively superficial within the carotid sheath. This is one of the most clinically important pulse points in the whole body, routinely checked in basic life support and cardiovascular examination. It corresponds to the common carotid artery just before it divides into internal and external branches.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The maxillary artery is a deep vessel of the face, not palpable in front of sternocleidomastoid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superficial temporal artery's pulse is felt in front of the ear, not in front of sternocleidomastoid.

questions.learning_objective: State that the carotid pulse, felt along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, is the common carotid artery.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.63

questions.title: Pulse at the base of the mandible
questions.question: The pulse felt at the base of the mandible is for which of these arteries?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The external carotid artery lies deeper and higher in the neck and is not itself the vessel palpated at the mandible's lower border.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The internal carotid artery has no accessible surface pulse at the mandible.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The common carotid artery's pulse is felt lower in the neck, alongside the larynx, not at the mandible.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The maxillary artery runs deep to the neck of the mandible, not superficially at its lower border.
explanations.E: Correct. The facial artery crosses superficially over the lower border of the mandible, just in front of the angle where the masseter muscle attaches, and its pulse can be readily felt at this point. This is the same crossing point clinicians use to control facial artery bleeding by direct pressure against the mandible. It is one of several standard head and neck pulse points, distinct from the carotid pulse felt lower in the neck and the superficial temporal pulse felt in front of the ear.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pulse felt at the lower border of the mandible is the facial artery.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.63

questions.title: Internal jugular vein's cranial origin
questions.question: The internal jagular vein begins as the continuation of …..

explanations.A: Correct. The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen at the base of the skull as the direct continuation of the sigmoid sinus, one of the dural venous sinuses draining blood from the brain. It descends through the neck within the carotid sheath, receiving tributaries including the inferior petrosal sinus, facial, lingual and pharyngeal veins along its course, before terminating by uniting with the subclavian vein. This cranial origin from the sigmoid sinus is the standard starting point for tracing the internal jugular vein's course.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior petrosal sinus is a tributary that joins the internal jugular vein near its origin, but the vein itself begins as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus, not the inferior petrosal sinus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The external jugular vein is an entirely separate, more superficial vein with no continuity with the internal jugular vein's origin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The subclavian vein is where the internal jugular vein terminates at its lower end, not where it begins at its upper end.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The brachiocephalic vein is formed by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins, downstream of the internal jugular vein's termination, not its point of origin.

questions.learning_objective: State that the internal jugular vein begins as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus at the jugular foramen.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.63

questions.title: Level of common carotid artery termination
questions.question: The level of termination of the common carotid artery is the disc between the …….. cervical vertebrae.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The disc between C2 and C3 is higher than the level at which the common carotid artery actually divides.
explanations.B: Correct. The common carotid artery ascends in the neck without giving off any branches and terminates by dividing into the internal and external carotid arteries at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, which corresponds to the intervertebral disc between the third and fourth cervical vertebrae (C3/C4). This bifurcation level is a key surgical and clinical landmark, marked by a dilation called the carotid sinus that houses baroreceptors. Levels above or below C3/C4 are commonly used as distractors for this fact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The disc between C4 and C5 is lower than the true bifurcation level.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The disc between C5 and C6 corresponds roughly to the cricoid cartilage, well below the true carotid bifurcation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The disc between C6 and C7 is near the origin of the common carotid artery from the brachiocephalic/subclavian vessels, far below its termination.

questions.learning_objective: State that the common carotid artery terminates (bifurcates) at the level of the C3/C4 intervertebral disc.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.63

questions.title: Structure running inside the carotid sheath
questions.question: Which one of the following structures runs inside the carotid sheath?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The external carotid artery lies outside the carotid sheath proper; the sheath's arterial content is the common and internal carotid arteries, not the external carotid.
explanations.B: Correct. The carotid sheath is a tubular condensation of deep cervical fascia enclosing the common carotid artery (and, above the bifurcation, the internal carotid artery), the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve, which runs in the groove between the artery and the vein. The internal jugular vein is therefore one of the sheath's three principal contents, running its whole length within it from the jugular foramen to its termination behind the clavicle. The external carotid artery, by contrast, lies outside the sheath once it branches off.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lingual artery is a branch of the external carotid artery running toward the tongue, outside the carotid sheath.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The subclavian vein lies at the root of the neck, separate from and not enclosed within the carotid sheath.

questions.learning_objective: State that the internal jugular vein is one of the carotid sheath's contents.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.65

questions.author_notes: Main concept reused from the Alexandria AU-MED-203 lane's own carotid-sheath concept (CON-NEU-A897156CACCE08, about the vagus nerve's course between the internal jugular vein and common carotid artery inside the sheath), which already establishes the internal jugular vein as a sheath content; see this lane's pending-live overlay.

questions.title: Artery arising from the medial aspect of the external carotid
questions.question: Which one of the following arteries arises from the medial aspect of the external carotid artery?

explanations.A: Correct. Most branches of the external carotid artery arise from its anterior (superior thyroid, lingual, facial), posterior (occipital, posterior auricular) or terminal aspects, but the ascending pharyngeal artery is the exception, arising instead from the artery's medial aspect close to its origin. It is a small vessel that ascends between the internal carotid artery and the pharynx to supply the pharynx, the prevertebral muscles, the middle ear and the meninges. This medial origin is the standard distinguishing fact tested for this particular branch.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The facial artery arises from the external carotid's anterior aspect, not its medial aspect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The occipital artery arises from the external carotid's posterior aspect, not its medial aspect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior auricular artery arises from the external carotid's posterior aspect, not its medial aspect.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superior thyroid artery arises from the external carotid's anterior aspect, not its medial aspect.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ascending pharyngeal artery is the exception among external carotid branches, arising from its medial rather than anterior or posterior aspect.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.65

questions.title: Retromandibular vein formation
questions.question: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of superficial temporal vein with which one of the following veins?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The infratrochlear vein is a small vein of the medial orbital region, not a tributary forming the retromandibular vein.
explanations.B: Correct. The retromandibular vein is formed within the substance of the parotid gland by the union of the superficial temporal vein with the maxillary vein, mirroring the arterial pattern in which the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries are the external carotid's own two terminal branches. The retromandibular vein then descends behind the mandible and splits into an anterior division, which joins the facial vein, and a posterior division, which joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein. Its formation from the superficial temporal and maxillary veins is therefore the direct venous counterpart of the arterial terminal-branch fact tested earlier in this lecture.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The occipital vein drains separately and is not one of the two veins forming the retromandibular vein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior auricular vein joins the retromandibular vein's posterior division further downstream, to help form the external jugular vein; it is not one of the two veins whose union forms the retromandibular vein itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The supraorbital vein contributes to the facial vein at the medial angle of the eye, not to the retromandibular vein.

questions.learning_objective: State that the retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.65

questions.title: Arterial supply of the upper lip
questions.question: The arterial supply of upper lip originates from which of the following arteries?

explanations.A: Correct. The upper lip is supplied by the superior labial branch of the facial artery, which runs a tortuous course close to the vermilion border, giving off septal and alar branches to the nose along the way. The facial artery similarly gives an inferior labial branch to the lower lip, so the facial artery is the source of arterial supply to both lips. This tortuous course of the facial artery near the mouth is also the anatomical reason lip lacerations bleed briskly and pulsate visibly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The occipital artery supplies the back of the scalp, not the lips.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior auricular artery supplies the area behind the ear, not the lips.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The supraorbital artery supplies the forehead and anterior scalp, not the lips.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The supratrochlear artery likewise supplies the forehead, not the lips.

questions.learning_objective: State that the facial artery, via its superior labial branch, supplies the upper lip.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.65

questions.title: Formation of the external jugular vein
questions.question: Which one of the followings share in the formation of the external jugular vein?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brachiocephalic vein is formed much further downstream, by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins, and does not itself contribute to forming the external jugular vein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Common lingual vein" is not a standard named tributary of the external jugular vein.
explanations.C: Correct. The external jugular vein is formed in the substance of the parotid gland, or just below it, by the union of the posterior division of the retromandibular vein with the posterior auricular vein. It then descends superficially across sternocleidomastoid to drain into the subclavian vein near the root of the neck. The retromandibular vein's posterior division is therefore one of the two vessels whose union directly forms the external jugular vein, complementing its anterior division, which instead joins the facial vein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sigmoid sinus is the intracranial origin of the internal jugular vein, an entirely separate vessel from the external jugular vein.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The subclavian vein is where the external jugular vein drains at its lower end, not one of the vessels forming it at its upper end.

questions.learning_objective: State that the retromandibular vein's posterior division joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.65

questions.title: Level of origin of the maxillary artery
questions.question: What is the level of origin of maxillary artery?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lower border of the hyoid bone is not the landmark used for the external carotid's terminal division.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lower border of the mandible is where the facial artery crosses onto the face, not where the maxillary artery originates.
explanations.C: Correct. The maxillary artery arises, together with the superficial temporal artery, from the terminal division of the external carotid artery behind the neck of the mandible, within the substance of the parotid gland. From there it runs forward, initially deep to the neck of the mandible, to reach the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae. This origin behind the neck of the mandible is the same landmark used for the external carotid's terminal division overall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sternoclavicular joint is a landmark used for structures at the root of the neck, unrelated to the maxillary artery's origin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The upper border of the thyroid cartilage is the landmark for the common carotid artery's bifurcation, not the maxillary artery's origin.

questions.learning_objective: State that the maxillary artery originates behind the neck of the mandible, at the external carotid's terminal division.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.66
